newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to introduce restrictive currency board.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to introduce restrictive currency board.

text.p: Bulgaria introduces a currency board system on Tuesday, confining itself to a monetary straitjacket in a last-ditch attempt to rescue the economy.

The currency board requires that levs in circulation and commercial banks' mimimum reserves at the central bank match central bank foreign exchange and gold reserves, effectively pegging the lev at a fixed exchange rate of 1,000 to the mark.
The mechanism is introduced for an indefinite period, and optimistic economists say its restrictions will bring Bulgaria close to the targets for joining the single European currency.
Currency boards have been used to repair crumbling financial systems and curb inflation in countries such as Argentina, Lithuania and Estonia. The system has also been proposed for Bosnia.
Imposition of a currency board stops governments from printing money which is not backed by reserves, and prevents the central bank from directly funding the budget deficit.
"It will put the government into such a steel straitjacket that it will squeeze it into behaving," said a Western banker.
Bulgaria has traditionally used on the dollar as the foreign currency benchmark, but demand for marks on the interbank market has risen since the announcement of the peg.
The International Monetary Fund proposed the mechanism for Bulgaria after the previous programme was suspended because the former Socialist government failed to meet its targets.

Bulgaria's economy ground to a halt last year after a run on the lev caused by the fragility of the banking sector and foreign exchange market. Interest rate increases failed to restore confidence, and once foreign exchange reserves were exhausted, the lev crashed.

A spiral of bad loans and refinancing in the banking sector was halted last year only when the central bank placed a third of the country's banks under supervision and started bankruptcy proceedings against them.
The government hopes to revive the banking sector by privatising the six biggest state banks by mid-1998.
Under the currency board the central bank has a new governor and deputy governors, who will operate three departments -- the Issue Department, Banking Department and Bank Supervision Department.
Refinancing is generally banned but the Banking Department may lend lev credit to a solvent bank for up to three months if there is a question of systemic risk.
The new central bank governor is Svetoslav Gavriiski, finance minister in the interim cabinet which governed between February and May and took the first stabilisation measures.
The interbank market will continue to operate with limits set for the lev to fluctuate on either side of the pegged rate. Interest rates will be set by the money market.

Bulgaria's foreign exchange reserves rose to 1.28 billion at the end of May compared to $600.2 million a year earlier, boosted by privatisations and foreign purchases of government bonds offering high yields with the security of the lev peg.
The government plans to issue mainly longer-term securities in the second half of the year to cover payments on the domestic debt, which reached 2.984 trillion levs at June 9.

Bulgaria will depend largely on privatisation income to meet budget requirements and to pay the interest and principal on its foreign debt over the next few years, though major foreign banks are discussing a Eurobond issue next year.
"They need to develop a strong export-led industrial base, cut bureaucracy and collect their taxes," said one banker. "It's a tall order."
